'''James Efflo Tyrer''' (February 25, 1939 – September 15, 1980) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was an [[offensive tackle]], widely regarded as one of the most dominant players of his era.<ref>{{Cite web |author=Gregorian |first=Vahe |date=2022-02-18 |title=Why aren't more past KC Chiefs stars (like Otis Taylor) enshrined in the Hall of Fame? |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/699510-kansas-city-chiefs-best-offensive-players-not-in-the-pro-football-hall-of-fame |website=Kansas City Star}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |author=Nix |first=JW |date=2011-05-03 |title=Kansas City Chiefs: Best Offensive Players Not in the Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/699510-kansas-city-chiefs-best-offensive-players-not-in-the-pro-football-hall-of-fa |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250106051512/https://bleacherreport.com/articles/699510-kansas-city-chiefs-best-offensive-players-not-in-the-pro-football-hall-of-fa |url-status=dead |archive-date=January 6, 2025 |access-date=2025-01-05 |website=Bleacher Report}}</ref> He played 14 years of professional football (1961 - 1974) after an All-American college career for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jim Tyrer Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TyreJi00.htm |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Kansas City Chiefs |url=https://archive.org/details/chiefs-1971-media-guide-kansas-city-c |title=Chiefs 1971 Media Guide (Kansas City) |date=August 1971}}</ref> competing in the [[American Football League]] (AFL) for the [[Dallas Texans (AFL)|Dallas Texans]] / [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and later in the [[National Football League]] (NFL): 13 years for Texans/Chiefs and his final year with the [[Washington Redskins]]. He was a nine-time Pro Bowl selection and a six-time first-team All-Pro.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Jim Tyrer Stats, Height, Weight, Position, Draft, College |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/TyreJi00.htm |access-date=2025-01-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> Standing 6'6" tall and weighing as much as 322 pounds during his career, Tyrer was known for his size, quick footwork, intelligence, and a notably large head, which he used to impose his will on opponents.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Turney |first=John |date=2019-05-13 |title=Pro Football Journal: The NFL's Best-ever Post-WWII Tackles |url=https://nflfootballjournal.blogspot.com/2019/05/the-nfls-best-ever-post-wwii-tackles.html |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Pro Football Journal}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Jul 23, 1973, page 12 - The Kansas City Star at Newspapers.com - Newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/676261613/?fcfToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJmcmVlLXZpZXctaWQiOjY3NjI2MTYxMywiaWF0IjoxNzM2MTM4NjMzLCJleHAiOjE3MzYyMjUwMzN9.ztvsmVlauN00w2FjWHJXhMFBt5Ho9b2e7_14NitQAUA |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=www.newspapers.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Reusse |first=Patrick |date=2020-11-15 |title=Tragedy, not Canton, became the fate of former Chiefs star lineman |url=https://www.startribune.com/tragedy-not-canton-became-the-fate-of-former-chiefs-star-lineman/573079201 |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=www.startribune.com |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Nix |first=J. W. |title=Pro Football Hall of Fame : The Best Players Not Yet Inducted at Each Position |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/809444-pro-football-hall-of-fame-the-best-players-not-yet-inducted-at-each-position |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Sep 21, 1980, page 28 - The Arizona Republic at Newspapers.com - Newspapers.com |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/120045726/?match=1&terms=Jim%20Tyrer%20intelligence |access-date=2025-01-07 |website=www.newspapers.com |language=en}}</ref>

A cornerstone of the Chiefs' success, owner [[Lamar Hunt]] credited him for helping establish Kansas City as a major sports town.<ref>{{Cite web |date=1977-02-07 |title=Tyrer Best Dish - All 280 Pounds |url=https://www.newspapers.com/image/677196062/?fcfToken=eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJmcmVlLXZpZXctaWQiOjY3NzE5NjA2MiwiaWF0IjoxNzM2MTk0ODUxLCJleHAiOjE3MzYyODEyNTF9.8zdQPC48B8SaXThXTykDoTmVeFUGDOWCX7EvZNU6D3s |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=www.newspapers.com |language=en}}</ref> He was a Chiefs team captain four years (1967 - 1971) including the team's [[Super Bowl IV]] championship season.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Judge |first=Clark |date=2024-07-22 |title=Maybe These AFL Stars Can Gain HOF Attention That Abner Haynes Did Not |url=https://talkoffametwo.com/nfl/afl-stars-not-in-hall-of-fame |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Talk of Fame |language=en}}</ref> Tyrer is often referenced as "the greatest player not in the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame|Hall of Fame]]," reflecting his lasting impact on the sport and much-debated omission from the Hall of Fame.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nix |first=J. W. |date=2011-05-13 |title=Kansas City Chiefs: Best Offensive Players Not in the Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/699510-kansas-city-chiefs-best-offensive-players-not-in-the-pro-football-hall-of-fame |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref>

He played in a period when linemen were prohibited from using their hands for blocking, and defensive players were permitted to use the "head slap" technique—a practice later outlawed due to its brutality.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Nix |first=J. W. |title=Crazy Canton Cuts: Jim Tyrer |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/389389-jim-tyrer |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Bleacher Report |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |date=2014-08-19 |title=NFL Rules Named After Players |url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2014/08/19/nfl-rules-and-the-players-who-inspired-them |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=SI |language=en-US}}</ref> Despite the physicality of the era and the demands of his position, Tyrer started 180 consecutive games, a then-record for the Chiefs, and every pre-season game (65) in his 13 years with the Texans/Chiefs franchise.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Official Website of the Kansas City Chiefs {{!}} Chiefs.com |url=https://www.chiefs.com/hallofhonor/players/jimtyrer |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=Kansas City Chiefs |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1973-07-23 |title=Tyrer Says 15 is Plenty |url=https://www.newspapers.com/article/the-kansas-city-star-tyrer-number-of-gam/95722585/ |access-date=2025-01-06 |work=The Kansas City Star |pages=12}}</ref> His 180 starts surpasses all left tackles in the Pro Football Hall of Fame as of 2024.

In the early morning hours of September 15, 1980, to the shock of the sports world, Tyrer murdered his wife, Martha, and then died by suicide.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Denlinger |first=Ken |date=1980-09-20 |title=Tyrer Tragedy: No Coping With Mortality |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1980/09/21/tyrer-tragedy-no-coping-with-mortality/7113d609-12c7-4532-ad03-1eafb4e85e8d/ |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]}}</ref> Teammate and author Michael Oriard would later describe Tyrer in the book "The End of Autumn" as "the unlikeliest suicide-murderer to those who knew him."<ref>{{Cite news |last=Socolow |first=Michael J. |date=2020-01-31 |title=Does Football Bear Responsibility for a Chiefs Legend's 1980 Murder-Suicide? |url=https://slate.com/culture/2020/01/jim-tyrer-chiefs-murder-suicide-wife-martha-cte.html |access-date=2025-01-06 |work=Slate |language=en-US |issn=1091-2339}}</ref>

Tyrer was a finalist for the Pro Football Hall of Fame at the time of the murder-suicide, his first year of eligibility. He did not advance in the selection process again for 44 years when research from ''Beneath the Shadow'' (a documentary by filmmaker Kevin Patrick Allen about Tyrer's life) led to a tacit acknowledgement from the PFHOF senior committee that Tyrer likely suffered from brain trauma.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Gregorian |first=Vahe |date=December 3, 2024 |title=How CTE explains why former KC Chiefs great Jim Tyrer is on cusp of Hall of Fame |url=https://www.kansascity.com/sports/spt-columns-blogs/vahe-gregorian/article296499024.html}}</ref> On December 3, 2024, Tyrer reached the finalist stage for the Pro Football Hall of Fame's Class of 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-12-03 |title=Contributor, coach, senior finalists revealed for Pro Football Hall of Fame Class of 2025 |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/contributor-coach-senior-finalists-revealed-for-pro-football-hall-of-fame-class-of-2025 |access-date=2025-01-06 |website=NFL.com |language=en-US}}</ref>

'''James Earl Johnson''' (March 31, 1938 – May 8, 2024) was an American professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1961 to 1976. He was named to the first team on the [[NFL 1970s All-Decade Team]], and in 1994, he was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]].

Johnson was born in [[Dallas]] and raised in [[Kingsburg, California]]. He was the younger brother of [[Rafer Johnson]], winner of the [[decathlon]] gold medal at the [[1960 Summer Olympics]]. Johnson played [[college football]] for the [[UCLA Bruins football|UCLA Bruins]] and was selected by the 49ers in the first round of the [[1961 NFL draft]]. He was selected four times as a first-team [[All-Pro]] and played in five [[Pro Bowl]]s. His jersey {{abbr|No.|number}} 37 was [[retired number|retired]] by the 49ers in 1977.

'''James Joseph Sorgi Jr.''' (born December 3, 1980) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[quarterback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]] and was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] in the sixth round of the [[2004 NFL draft]]. Sorgi served as the backup to [[Peyton Manning]] for several years, and won a ring when the Colts won [[Super Bowl XLI]]. Once he was released by the Colts, he signed with the [[New York Giants]] as the backup to [[Eli Manning]], but was injured in a preseason game, and was placed on IR.

'''James Whittington "Jimbo" Elrod''' (May 25, 1954 – December 12, 2016) was an American professional [[American football|football]] [[linebacker]] who was an [[All-American]] at the [[University of Oklahoma]] and played professionally for the [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and the [[History of the Tennessee Titans|Houston Oilers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL).

Elrod graduated from [[East Central High School (Oklahoma)|East Central High School]] in [[Tulsa, Oklahoma]], in 1972 and was a member of the [[NCAA Division I FBS National Football Championship|National Championship]] football teams of [[1974 Oklahoma Sooners football team|1974]] and [[1975 Oklahoma Sooners football team|1975]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.soonersports.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/aa-jimbo-elrod-1975.html |title=Sooner Sports.com |access-date=2009-03-27 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090222223939/http://www.soonersports.com/sports/m-footbl/archive/aa-jimbo-elrod-1975.html |archive-date=2009-02-22 |url-status=dead }}</ref> 
Elrod earned consensus [[1975 College Football All-America Team|All-America]] honors in 1975, when he had 20 [[Tackle (football move)|tackles]] for loss. His 44 tackles for loss led the career list at the University of Oklahoma until 2001 (it now stands as sixth-best all-time).

Elrod starred in the [[1976 Orange Bowl]] a 14–6 victory over the [[University of Michigan]] that secured the Sooners a fifth national championship. The Oklahoma defense allowed only 202 total yards in the game. He was drafted by the Kansas City Chiefs in the 5th round (144th overall) of the [[1976 NFL draft]] where he played three seasons and in 1979 he played one season with the Oilers.

He earned a dual scholarship to the University of Oklahoma, where he was a member of the 1974 National Championship Wrestling team. Elrod earned a degree in public relations and business administration and after his NFL career he worked in the personal health care business and well as radio hosting and analysis.<ref>[http://www.kokcradio.com/totalsports.aspx KOKC Radio.com] {{Dead link|date=February 2020 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Elrod later became a radio talk show host at [[KOKC (AM)]] 1520, the flagship station for the University of Oklahoma located in Oklahoma City.

Elrod was killed in a car accident on December 12, 2016.<ref>{{cite web | last=Daniels | first=Tim | title=Former Oklahoma All-American Jimbo Elrod Dies at 62 | website=Bleacher Report | date=12 December 2016 | url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/2681396-former-oklahoma-all-american-jimbo-elrod-dies-at-62 | access-date=12 December 2023}}</ref>

'''James Garoppolo''' (born November 2, 1991), nicknamed "'''Jimmy G'''",<ref>{{Cite web |last=Bernstein |first=Dan |date=October 18, 2020 |title=Jimmy Garoppolo's nicknames, ranked: From Jimmy G to Gucci Garopp |url=https://www.sportingnews.com/us/nfl/news/jimmy-garoppolo-nicknames-ranked/1owu62hp87ygl1wvkpuypdp98u |access-date=May 3, 2021 |website=The Sporting News |language=en |archive-date=May 3, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210503053717/https://www.sportingnews.com/us/nfl/news/jimmy-garoppolo-nicknames-ranked/1owu62hp87ygl1wvkpuypdp98u |url-status=live }}</ref> is an American professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Eastern Illinois Panthers football|Eastern Illinois Panthers]], setting school records for career passing yards and passing touchdowns and winning the [[Walter Payton Award]] as a senior.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Huguenin |first=Mike |date=October 30, 2013 |title=Tony Romo, Sean Payton have praise for QB Jimmy Garoppolo |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/tony-romo-sean-payton-have-prais-for-qb-jimmy-garoppolo-0ap2000000273634 |access-date=September 19, 2019 |website=NFL.com |archive-date=January 15, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200115230508/http://www.nfl.com/news/story/0ap2000000273634/article/tony-romo-sean-payton-have-prais-for-qb-jimmy-garoppolo |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Bogard |first=Catlin |date=September 28, 2013 |title=EIU QB Jimmy Garoppolo breaks TD, Yards record |url=http://ovcball.net/2013/09/eiu-qb-jimmy-garoppolo-breaks-td-record/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20141214215900/http://ovcball.net/2013/09/eiu-qb-jimmy-garoppolo-breaks-td-record/ |archive-date=December 14, 2014 |access-date=February 14, 2019 |website=OVCBall.net}}</ref><ref name="WalterPayton">{{Cite web |date=December 16, 2013 |title=Eastern Illinois QB Jimmy Garoppolo wins Walter Payton Award |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/eastern-illinois-qb-jimmy-garoppolo-wins-walter-payton-award-0ap2000000299934 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210929192028/https://www.nfl.com/news/eastern-illinois-qb-jimmy-garoppolo-wins-walter-payton-award-0ap2000000299934 |archive-date=September 29, 2021 |access-date=September 29, 2021 |website=NFL.com}}</ref> Garoppolo was selected in the second round of the [[2014 NFL draft]] by the [[New England Patriots]], where he spent his first four seasons as [[Tom Brady]]'s backup and was a member of two [[Super Bowl]]-winning teams.

Traded to the [[San Francisco 49ers]] near the end of the 2017 season, Garoppolo helped revitalize a 1–10 team by winning the last five games of the season. His most successful season was in 2019 when he guided the 49ers to the #1-seed in the NFC and an appearance in [[Super Bowl LIV]]. Garoppolo also helped lead them to an [[NFC Championship Game]] appearance in 2021. However, his San Francisco tenure was afflicted by injuries, which caused him to miss most of the 2018 and 2020 seasons. After suffering another season-ending injury in 2022, Garoppolo spent the following season with the [[Las Vegas Raiders]] before joining the [[Los Angeles Rams]] in 2024.

'''James Frederick Thrower''' (born November 6, 1947) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[defensive back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[East Texas State Lions football|East Texas State Lions]] (now East Texas A&M). In 2022 he was inducted into the Arkansas Black Hall of Fame.<ref name=hof>{{Cite web|url=http://www.magnoliareporter.com/living_and_learning/community_groups/article_2f495dce-2ea2-11ed-ad8b-dbee26a5746e.html|title=Ketty Lester, James Thrower among Arkansas Black Hall of Fame inductees|date=September 9, 2022|website=Magnolia Reporter - Magnolia, Arkansas News}}</ref>

Thrower was born in [[Camden, Arkansas]], in 1947. He attended Lincoln High School and played college football at [[East Texas State University]].<ref name=PFR/> He also excelled at track and field and basketball, and was inducted into the university's athletic hall of fame.<ref name=hof/>

Thrower played professional football as a defensive back in the NFL for the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] from 1970 to 1972.<ref name=PFR/><ref>{{cite news|title=No Prevent Defense For Thrower's Boos|newspaper=Philadelphia Daily News|author=Bill Shefski|date=October 18, 1972|page=60|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/109779873/no-prevent-defense-for-throwers-boos/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|title=Eagles Try Jim Thrower Where Others Have Failed|newspaper=The Philadelphia Inquirer|author=Gordon Forbes|date=December 8, 1970|page=25|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/109780318/jim-thrower/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>  He was fired by the Eagles in November 1972.<ref>{{cite news|title=Eagles Fire Thrower Just As Tipster Warned|newspaper=Philadelphia Daily News|date=November 3, 1972|page=82|author=Bill Shefski|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/109780152/jim-thrower/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

He next played for the [[Detroit Lions]] during the 1973 and 1974 seasons.<ref name=PFR/> While with the Lions, he was a backup to cornerback [[Lem Barney]] and also served as captain of the special team unit.  He was also a member of the Fellowship of Christian Athletes.<ref>{{cite news|title=Thrower Is A Lion . . . Detroit Variety|newspaper=The Ludington Daily News|author=Richard L. Dancz|date=June 5, 1975|page=6|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/109779571/jim-thrower/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref> During the 1975, was placed on the injured reserve list. The ''Detroit Free Press'' called him the captain of the injured reserve list.<ref>{{cite news|title=Injured Lions Have Their Own Captain|newspaper=Detroit Free Press|author=Jack Saylor|date=November 21, 1975|page=11|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/109780540/jim-thrower/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>

In three years in the NFL, Thrower appeared in a total of 46 NFL games, four of them as a starter.<ref name=PFR>{{cite web|title=Jim Thrower|publisher=Sports Reference LLC|work=Pro-Football-Reference.com|accessdate=November 2, 2020|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/T/ThroJi20.htm}}</ref>

After retiring from football, Thrower worked for the Stroh Brewery Co. and later Michigan Consolidated Gas Co. He was also a leading fundraiser for the [[NAACP]].<ref>{{cite news|title=Former star athlete still seeks big play|newspaper=Detroit Free Press|author=Susan Watson|date=August 21, 1985|page=A3|url=https://www.newspapers.com/clip/62645178/former-star-athlete-still-seeks-big-play/|via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref>
